name: Lipnice Castle
region: Vysočina Region — Lipnice nad Sázavou, Havlíčkův Brod District
address: Hrad Lipnice, Lipnice nad Sázavou, 582 32, Czech Republic
architectural_style: Early 14th-century Bohemian Gothic castle, now partially ruined — founded in the early 14th century by the Lichtenburk family as one of the most ambitious royal-quality castle projects in Bohemia; the complex includes the large Samson Tower (Samsonova věž), one of the best-preserved parts of the fortification, named after a carved Samson relief; the original Gothic fortress incorporated a great hall, residential palaces, and a sophisticated gate system; much of the complex was damaged in the 15th century during the Hussite wars and progressive later ruination left large sections as picturesque ruin; the Samson Tower and parts of the curtain wall circuit have been stabilised for visitor access, with panoramic views from the tower over the Vysočina countryside and the Sázava river valley

opening_hours.seasonal_note: Open Tuesday–Sunday May through September; reduced days in April and October (weekends only); closed November through March. Guided tours of the castle interior run at scheduled intervals. Confirm current dates and times at hrad-lipnice.cz or via the GYG ticket before visiting. The Samson Tower view terrace is accessible with the standard admission.

visit_duration: 1–1.5 hours (guided tour of the castle complex, Samson Tower, and courtyard ruins)
best_season: May to September — the Vysočina landscape is at its most attractive in late spring and summer; the castle season runs May–September with full hours. October visits are possible on weekends but hours are reduced.
accessibility: The castle complex involves uneven stone surfaces and stairs, including a climb of the Samson Tower. Not wheelchair accessible. The access path from the village of Lipnice nad Sázavou involves a moderate uphill walk.
tagline: One of Bohemia's largest medieval castles — and the Vysočina village where Jaroslav Hašek wrote *The Good Soldier Švejk* and spent his final years
highlights: Jaroslav Hašek and The Good Soldier Švejk — one of the 20th century's great anti-war novels — Czech writer Jaroslav Hašek (1883–1923) moved to Lipnice nad Sázavou in 1921 and spent the last two years of his life there, writing in a local pub; he died in Lipnice in January 1923 and is buried in the village churchyard; The Good Soldier Švejk (Osudy dobrého vojáka Švejka), the satirical novel he was working on in Lipnice, is one of the most widely read Czech novels internationally and one of the defining works of literary anti-militarism

Samson Tower — panoramic Vysočina viewpoint — the Samson Tower (Samsonova věž) is the best-preserved element of the medieval fortification, named after a carved Samson relief on the tower; from its top, the view extends over the Sázava river valley and the rolling Vysočina countryside — a characteristically Czech Highlands landscape of fields, forests, and villages that Hašek found restful after years of upheaval

One of Bohemia's largest early Gothic castle complexes — founded in the early 14th century by the Lichtenburk family, Lipnice was one of the most ambitious Bohemian castle projects of its era, comparable in scale to the great royal and magnate fortresses of 14th-century Bohemia; the complex included a great hall, residential palaces, a sophisticated gate system, and extensive curtain walls before later damage left it partially ruined

Hussite Wars damage and picturesque ruination — the castle was significantly damaged during the Hussite movement of the 15th century, when Bohemia experienced some of the most destructive religious and military conflict in its medieval history; the picturesque ruin character of Lipnice today reflects centuries of partial collapse and stabilisation rather than systematic demolition

A literary pilgrimage site for Good Soldier Švejk readers — the village of Lipnice nad Sázavou preserves Hašek's memory through a small museum in the house where he lived, the pub where he wrote (still operating), and his grave in the churchyard; for readers of Švejk, a visit to Lipnice Castle includes a walk through the village that makes the context of his final years and the novel's unfinished character physically concrete
description:
The hill above Lipnice nad Sázavou was chosen as a castle site for the same reason that most hill sites in medieval Bohemia were chosen: it was defensible, it commanded the surrounding country, and the approach from any direction involved an uphill walk that gave the defenders time and advantage. The Lichtenburk family, who founded the castle in the early 14th century, were a significant noble house in the Bohemian political landscape of the period, and they built at Lipnice on a scale appropriate to their ambitions — a complex of great hall, residential palace, gate system, and curtain walls that made Lipnice one of the most substantial Gothic castle projects of its era in Bohemia.

The castle's history across the medieval period was complex and violent. The Hussite movement of the 15th century — a religious reform and military revolt that made Bohemia the scene of some of the most sustained conflict in late medieval Central Europe — swept through the Vysočina region, and Lipnice was drawn into the fighting. The castle changed hands, was damaged, was repaired, changed hands again. The sequence of ownership that followed the Hussite period carried the castle through the 16th and 17th centuries in various states of maintenance, until it began the decline into ruin that characterises its current condition.

What remains today is substantial enough to give a clear picture of the original ambition. The Samson Tower — the best-preserved element of the fortification, named for a carved relief of Samson that decorates its exterior — rises to a height that commands the surrounding Vysočina countryside, and the view from its top is one of the better castle panoramas in the Czech Highlands: the Sázava river valley below, the rolling fields and forested hillsides stretching to the horizon, the village of Lipnice in the foreground. The great courtyard of the original complex is largely open ruin, the outlines of the vanished halls and palaces traceable in the foundations and stub walls that survive. The curtain wall circuit, partially restored and partially in its ruined state, encloses the complex.

The reason most visitors give for seeking out Lipnice, however, is literary. Jaroslav Hašek, the Czech writer who created *Osudy dobrého vojáka Švejka* (The Good Soldier Švejk), moved to the village of Lipnice nad Sázavou in 1921 after years of extraordinary biographical chaos — he had lived through the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, fought on multiple sides of the Russian Civil War, married twice (simultaneously, technically), run a dog-breeding scheme, edited anarchist newspapers, and led a life of spectacular disorder. In Lipnice, he found something closer to stability. He settled in a local pub known as Na Čáslavce, established himself as part of village life, and wrote.

The Good Soldier Švejk is the satirical novel that came out of this period: a sprawling, episodic, deliberately unfinished account of Josef Švejk, an apparently simple-minded Czech soldier navigating the bureaucratic and military absurdities of the Austro-Hungarian Empire during the First World War. Whether Švejk's idiocy is genuine or performed is left deliberately unclear; what is clear is that the world around him is comprehensively ridiculous, and that the structures of military authority, nationalism, and official procedure are the proper objects of satire. The novel was left unfinished — Hašek died in Lipnice in January 1923 at the age of 39, with the fourth volume incomplete. He is buried in the village churchyard, a short walk from the pub where he wrote.

For readers of Švejk — and there are many, in many languages — Lipnice is a minor but genuine pilgrimage destination. A small museum in the house where Hašek lived preserves materials from his time there; the pub where he wrote is still operational. The castle above the village is the landscape backdrop for the literary visit, and stands in its own right as one of the larger Gothic castle ruins in the Czech Highlands.

The GYG private tour from Prague (t1192443) includes transport, a guide, entrance to the castle, and lunch — making it a complete day trip for visitors who want to combine the castle visit with a guide to the Hašek connection without individual logistics.

[Konopište Castle](/castles/czech-republic/konopiste-castle) — the hunting château rebuilt by Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria in the late 19th century, approximately 80km northwest of Lipnice — is the major Central Bohemia château destination and the standard comparison point for visitors exploring the region.
history: Early 14th century: Lichtenburk family founds Lipnice Castle as one of the most ambitious Gothic castle projects of its era in Bohemia. 14th–early 15th century: castle passes through successive Bohemian noble families; a significant fortification and residential complex. 15th century: Hussite Wars — castle caught in the conflict; significantly damaged and changes hands multiple times. 16th–17th century: progressive decline; various owners attempt maintenance but the complex begins its long ruination. 17th–19th century: castle increasingly ruined; picturesque character noted by Romantic-era visitors. 1921: Jaroslav Hašek moves to Lipnice nad Sázavou; writes parts of The Good Soldier Švejk in the village pub. January 1923: Hašek dies in Lipnice aged 39; buried in the village churchyard; the Švejk novel is left unfinished. 20th century: castle conserved and stabilised by the Czechoslovak state; Samson Tower renovated for visitor access. Present day: open May–September, Tuesday–Sunday; guided tours and Samson Tower views.
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** Lipnice nad Sázavou is about 110 km east-southeast of Prague (D1 motorway then local roads, ~1.5 hours by car). Public transport is limited; the most practical option without a car is a train to Havlíčkův Brod (served from Prague), then a taxi for the final 20 km.

**Tickets:** Walk-up entry is €8 adult, €4 child; open Tuesday–Sunday May–September (weekends only in April and October). The GYG private day trip from Prague (t1192443, from €297, new — no reviews yet) includes private transport, a specialist guide, castle entrance, and lunch.

**Practical tips:** The castle visit pairs naturally with a Hašek literary walk through the village — the museum in his house, the pub Na Čáslavce where he wrote, and his grave in the churchyard. Allow a full half-day for the castle and village together rather than treating Lipnice as a quick stop.

**Combine with:** [Konopiště Castle](/castles/czech-republic/konopiste-castle) — the hunting château of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, 80 km northwest on a return route toward Prague.

faqs.question: Who was Jaroslav Hašek and why is Lipnice associated with him?
faqs.answer: Jaroslav Hašek (1883–1923) was a Czech writer best known for The Good Soldier Švejk (Osudy dobrého vojáka Švejka), a satirical anti-war novel following an apparently simple-minded Czech soldier through the absurdities of Austro-Hungarian military bureaucracy during the First World War. Hašek lived a legendarily chaotic life — anarchist agitator, bigamist, dog-breeder, veteran of multiple armies — before settling in the village of Lipnice nad Sázavou in 1921, where he found relative stability and wrote parts of Švejk in a local pub. He died in Lipnice in January 1923 at 39, leaving the fourth volume of Švejk unfinished. He is buried in the village churchyard. Lipnice has a small Hašek museum and the original pub where he wrote is still in operation.

faqs.question: What is the Samson Tower and what can I see from it?
faqs.answer: The Samson Tower (Samsonova věž) is the best-preserved part of Lipnice Castle, named after a carved relief of the biblical figure Samson on the tower's exterior. It is the dominant element of the surviving fortification and offers the most rewarding views from the site — the Sázava river valley to the east, the rolling Vysočina countryside in all directions, and the village of Lipnice below. The tower can be climbed as part of the standard guided tour; it involves stairs and is accessible for most visitors with reasonable mobility.

faqs.question: How does Lipnice Castle compare to other Czech castle ruins?
faqs.answer: Lipnice was founded as one of the more ambitious Gothic castle projects in Bohemia in the early 14th century, comparable in original scale to major Bohemian fortifications of the same era. In its current state as a partially stabilised ruin, it is less dramatically positioned than some Czech castle ruins (Kokorin on its sandstone promontory, Vranov rising from the river gorge) but more historically substantial in its surviving fabric. The combination of a genuine large-scale Gothic ruin with the specific Hašek literary connection makes Lipnice distinctive among Czech castle visits in the way that few purely architectural visits can be: the landscape has a biographical dimension that the castle itself provides the physical backdrop for.
